name: Triangular Number
description: Computes the nth triangular number, the sum of all integers from 1 to n, using the closed form n(n+1)/2. It counts objects arranged in a triangle with n rows.
notes: The index n should be a non-negative integer. The product n(n+1) is always even, so the result is always a whole number.

name: Sum of Squares 1 to n (Closed Form)
description: Computes the sum of the squares of the integers from 1 to n using the closed form n(n+1)(2n+1)/6. It replaces adding 1^2 + 2^2 + ... + n^2 term by term.
notes: The index n should be a positive integer. The numerator is always divisible by 6, so the result is an exact whole number.

name: Sum of Cubes 1 to n (Closed Form)
description: Computes the sum of the cubes of the integers from 1 to n as the square of the nth triangular number, (n(n+1)/2)^2. This reflects the identity that the sum of cubes equals the square of the sum.
notes: The index n should be a positive integer. The result equals (1+2+...+n) squared, a perfect square.

name: Sum of First n Fourth Powers
description: Computes the sum of the fourth powers of the integers from 1 to n using the closed form n(n+1)(2n+1)(3n^2+3n-1)/30. It replaces adding 1^4 + 2^4 + ... + n^4 directly.
notes: The index n should be a positive integer. The numerator is always divisible by 30, so the exact result is a whole number.

name: Pentagonal Number
description: Computes the nth pentagonal number using n(3n-1)/2. These figurate numbers count dots forming nested pentagons and give the sequence 1, 5, 12, 22, and so on.
notes: This uses positive index n for standard pentagonal numbers. Generalized pentagonal numbers use negative indices too, which this form also handles algebraically.

name: Hexagonal Number
description: Computes the nth hexagonal number using n(2n-1). These figurate numbers count dots forming nested hexagons and give the sequence 1, 6, 15, 28, and so on.
notes: The index n should be a positive integer. Every hexagonal number is also a triangular number (specifically the (2n-1)th one).

name: Tetrahedral Number
description: Computes the nth tetrahedral number using n(n+1)(n+2)/6, the number of spheres stacked in a triangular pyramid with n layers. It equals the running sum of the first n triangular numbers.
notes: The index n should be a positive integer. The product of three consecutive integers is always divisible by 6, so the result is a whole number.

name: Sum of the First n Odd Integers
description: Returns the sum of the first n odd integers (1 + 3 + 5 + ... ), which equals n squared. Adding the first n odd numbers always produces a perfect square.
notes: Here n is the count of odd terms summed, not the largest odd number. The result is exactly n^2 for any positive integer n.

name: Sum of First n Even Numbers
description: Returns the sum of the first n even integers (2 + 4 + 6 + ... ), which equals n(n+1). It is twice the nth triangular number.
notes: Here n is the count of even terms summed. The result equals n(n+1), always an even number for positive integer n.

name: Arithmetic Series Sum (First and Last Term)
description: Sums an arithmetic series of n terms by averaging the first and last terms and multiplying by the number of terms: n(a+l)/2. It works for any arithmetic progression whose endpoints are known.
notes: It requires the series to be arithmetic (constant difference) and needs the actual last term l, not the common difference. All n terms must lie between a and l.

name: Finite Geometric Series Sum (First n Terms)
description: Sums the first n terms of a geometric series with first term a and common ratio r using a(1-r^n)/(1-r). It gives the total of a + ar + ar^2 + ... + ar^(n-1).
notes: The ratio r must not equal 1, or the formula divides by zero; for r = 1 the sum is simply n times a. For |r| below 1 and large n the sum approaches a/(1-r).

name: Least Common Multiple (from GCD)
description: Computes the least common multiple of two integers as their product divided by their greatest common divisor, a*b/g. It uses the identity that lcm times gcd equals the product of the numbers.
notes: The value g must be the correct greatest common divisor of a and b; an incorrect g gives a wrong result. Works for positive integers.

name: Euler Totient of a Prime Power
description: Computes Euler's totient of a prime power p^k, the count of integers up to p^k that are coprime to it, using p^k - p^(k-1). It equals p^k times (1 - 1/p).
notes: This form is valid only when p is prime; for composite bases the totient formula differs. The exponent k should be a positive integer.

name: Euler Totient of a Semiprime
description: Computes Euler's totient of a product of two distinct primes as (p-1)(q-1), the count of integers up to pq that are coprime to it. This value underpins the RSA cryptosystem.
notes: Both p and q must be prime and distinct for this formula; if p equals q the correct totient is p(p-1) instead. The result is the number of units modulo pq.

name: Divisor Count (Two Prime Factors)
description: Counts the divisors of a number whose prime factorization is p^a times q^b, using (a+1)(b+1). Each exponent can independently range from 0 up to its maximum, giving the total divisor count.
notes: This applies only to numbers with exactly two distinct prime factors; a and b are the exponents in the factorization, not the primes themselves. Include 1 and the number itself in the count.

name: Sum of Divisors of a Prime Power
description: Computes the sum of all divisors of a prime power p^k using the geometric series (p^(k+1)-1)/(p-1). This adds 1 + p + p^2 + ... + p^k, all divisors of p^k.
notes: Valid only when p is prime; the divisors of p^k are exactly the powers of p up to k. Requires p greater than 1 so the denominator is nonzero.

name: Prime Counting Function Approximation (PNT)
description: Approximates the number of primes not exceeding x as x divided by the natural log of x, the leading term of the prime number theorem. It estimates prime density for large x.
notes: This is an asymptotic estimate that is rough for small x and consistently undercounts; the logarithmic integral Li(x) is more accurate. Requires x greater than 1.

name: nth Prime Number Approximation
description: Approximates the value of the nth prime number using n times (ln n + ln ln n). It gives a rough estimate of how large the nth prime is for moderately large n.
notes: It is asymptotic and inaccurate for small n; it requires n large enough that ln(ln(n)) is defined and positive (n above roughly 15). The true nth prime differs by lower-order terms.

name: Number of Digits (Base 10)
description: Returns the number of decimal digits in a positive integer n as the floor of its base-10 logarithm plus one. For example, 12345 has floor(4.09)+1 = 5 digits.
notes: Here log is the base-10 logarithm and n must be a positive integer. Exact powers of ten sit on the boundary, so floating-point rounding can occasionally shift the count.

name: Digit Count of n! (Stirling)
expression: floor(0.5 * log(2 * pi * n) + n * log(n / e)) + 1
description: Estimates the number of decimal digits in n factorial using Stirling's approximation for log(n!), taking the floor and adding one. It lets you gauge the size of a factorial without computing it.
notes: log here is base 10. The result is an approximation and can be off by one near boundaries; it is most reliable for larger n.

name: Stirling's Factorial Approximation
description: Approximates n factorial with Stirling's formula, sqrt(2*pi*n) times (n/e)^n. It gives a fast estimate of the factorial that grows increasingly accurate in relative terms as n grows.
notes: The relative error shrinks with larger n but the absolute value is only approximate; it always slightly underestimates n!. Requires n positive.

name: Stirling Log-Factorial Approximation
expression: n * ln(n) - n + 0.5 * ln(2 * pi * n)
description: Approximates the natural logarithm of n factorial using n*ln(n) - n + 0.5*ln(2*pi*n). This is the logarithmic form of Stirling's formula, useful when n! itself is too large to store.
notes: This returns ln(n!), not n! itself; exponentiate to recover the factorial. Uses natural log, and accuracy improves with larger n.

name: Harmonic Number Approximation (Euler-Mascheroni)
description: Approximates the nth harmonic number (1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/n) as ln(n) plus the Euler-Mascheroni constant plus 1/(2n). It closely estimates the harmonic sum without adding each term.
notes: gamma is the Euler-Mascheroni constant, about 0.5772. The 1/(2n) correction makes it accurate for moderate n; accuracy improves as n grows.

name: Central Binomial Coefficient (Asymptotic)
description: Approximates the central binomial coefficient C(2n, n) as 4^n divided by sqrt(pi*n). It estimates the largest coefficient in the 2n-th row of Pascal's triangle for large n.
notes: This is an asymptotic approximation derived from Stirling's formula and slightly overestimates; accuracy improves as n grows. Here n is half the top index (2n choose n).

name: Catalan Number (Asymptotic)
description: Approximates the nth Catalan number as 4^n divided by ((n+1) times sqrt(pi*n)). Catalan numbers count many combinatorial structures such as balanced parentheses and binary trees.
notes: This is an asymptotic estimate that improves with larger n and is not exact; round to compare with the true integer Catalan number. Requires n at least 1.

name: Lucas Number (Closed Form)
description: Computes the nth Lucas number in closed form as Phi^n plus cos(n*pi)/Phi^n, where Phi is the golden ratio. The cosine term equals (-1)^n, reproducing the alternating psi^n contribution.
notes: Phi must be the golden ratio, about 1.618034; cos(n*pi) gives (-1)^n for integer n. Floating-point error can require rounding to get the exact integer Lucas number.

name: Basel Series Tail Approximation
description: Approximates the partial sum of the Basel series (sum of 1/k^2) after n terms as its limit pi^2/6 minus 1/n. It estimates how close the truncated sum is to its known total.
notes: pi^2/6 is the exact infinite sum; subtracting 1/n approximates the remaining tail. The estimate improves for larger n and is not the exact partial sum.

name: Euler's Number via Compound Limit
description: Evaluates (1 + 1/n)^n, the classic expression whose limit as n grows without bound is Euler's number e. Larger n brings the value closer to e, matching continuous compounding.
notes: This is a finite-n approximation that converges slowly to e and always stays below it. Larger n improves accuracy but eventually meets floating-point limits.

name: Wallis Product nth Factor
description: Computes the nth factor of the Wallis product, (2n/(2n-1))*(2n/(2n+1)). Multiplying these factors over successive n converges to pi/2, giving an infinite product for pi.
notes: This returns a single factor, not the accumulated product; multiply factors from 1 to n and double the result to approach pi. Each factor is slightly greater than 1.
